name: MIC2779L-2YM5-TR
title: MIC2779: battery voltage monitor with separately set low and high thresholds, push-pull reset, SOT23-5
summary: A low-power voltage monitor with two comparator inputs against a 1.240 V bandgap: LTH sets the level at which the reset output trips and latches, HTH the higher level at which it lets go, so the hysteresis is set by an external three-resistor divider. Once HTH has risen past the reference, the output stays asserted for 140 ms minimum before releasing. The supply pin is separate from the sensing inputs, the output is push-pull, and supply current is 1 µA typical. MIC2779L has an active-low /RST and MIC2779H an active-high RST; both are 2 % parts in a 5-lead SOT23 for -40 °C to +85 °C.
key_figures: 1 µA typ, 2 µA max (output not asserted)
1.5 V to 5.5 V; output held low down to VDD = 1.2 V
push-pull; L: active-low /RST, H: active-high RST

notes: Code fields in order: H or L for polarity, -2 for 2 % accuracy, Y for the temperature range, M5 for the package, -TR for tape and reel.
The -TR suffix is an ordering code only and does not appear in the marking on the part.

Top mark: a product code on the first line and a three-character traceability code on the second (for instance UPB1 over 288). The package is Pb-free; its JEDEC e3 (matte tin) mark is on the outer packing.

circuits.title: Cellular telephone battery monitor
circuits.description: A single Li-ion cell feeds a 3.0 V LDO and also powers the MIC2779L directly. A divider of 604 kΩ, 56 kΩ and 340 kΩ from the cell to ground drives LTH from its upper tap and HTH from its lower tap, giving VBAT(hi) = 3.6 V and VBAT(lo) = 3.1 V. /RST drives the LDO's enable, so the 3.0 V rail is switched off once the cell falls to 3.1 V and comes back after the cell has passed 3.6 V and the reset delay has run.

circuits.title: Example circuit
circuits.description: The three-resistor divider on its own: R1 from VBATT to the LTH tap, R2 from the LTH tap to the HTH tap, R3 from the HTH tap to ground. VBATT also supplies VDD, and the reset pin is the circuit's output (/RST on the L part, RST on the H part).

where.R1: divider resistor from VBAT to the LTH tap
where.R2: divider resistor between the LTH and HTH taps
where.R3: divider resistor from the HTH tap to ground

equations.name: Worked example, R2 and R1
equations.note: The circuits use 604 kΩ, 56 kΩ and 340 kΩ, 1 %.

operation.text: The part watches a battery through a divider. When the cell runs down past the lower set point the output asserts. After the cell is swapped or recharged above the upper set point, the output stays asserted (low on the L part, high on the H part) for at least 140 ms and then releases.
The reset output drives both ways (push-pull) at logic levels. MIC2779L drives /RST, active low; MIC2779H drives RST, active high. For an open-drain output the MIC2778 or MIC833 is the alternative.

Each input goes to a comparator against the internal reference. VLTH falling under VREF asserts the output, and at that moment VHTH is taken to be under VREF as well. The asserted state is latched, so recovery of the cell or removal of the load cannot make the output toggle; only VHTH rising above VREF ends it.
At power-up, or after the cell is replaced or recharged, VHTH crossing above VREF starts a delay; the output is released after 140 ms minimum (420 ms maximum).
VDD is separate from the sensing inputs, so the part may run from a rail downstream of the battery such as a boost converter output. Supply current is 1 µA typical.

Fix the divider total R1 + R2 + R3 first; 1 MΩ keeps battery drain low with no measurable loss of accuracy. Leakage into a high-value divider shifts the trip points, and the total from VBAT to ground should stay at 3 MΩ or less. Set VBAT(HI) first to get R3, then use VBAT(LO) to get R2, and R1 is what remains. For one Li-ion cell, 3.6 V is a sensible upper point (moderately charged); the cell must not go below 2.5 V and many designs stop at 3.1 V. Resistor tolerance follows the accuracy the system needs.

Brief negative-going dips below VBAT(LO) are ignored: the narrower the dip, the larger the overdrive below VREF it can have without causing a reset. Typical longest ignored dip is about 115 µs at 3.6 mV overdrive, 36 µs at 32 mV and 12 µs at 180 to 360 mV.
